summary: This informational memo evaluates how well SNMP, RSIP, Megaco, Diameter and COPS could serve as the protocol for middlebox communications, which lets applications talk to devices like firewalls. It compares each candidate against the requirements.

eli5.summary: Applications sometimes need to ask a firewall for help. This document compares several existing ways to ask and judges which fit best.

questions: which protocol was best for midcom
subtitle: A scorecard of five existing protocols against the requirements for talking to firewalls and NATs.

tldr.problem: The MIDCOM working group needed a protocol that lets an application-aware agent control middleboxes such as firewalls and NATs, and had to choose one rather than invent a new one.
tldr.mechanism: Volunteers wrote evaluations of SNMP, RSIP, Megaco, Diameter and COPS. Each protocol was scored requirement by requirement as totally compliant, partially compliant with extensions, partially compliant, or failing.
tldr.outcome: None of the five failed any requirement. SNMP scored best with 22 fully met, RSIP was not accepted by the working group because of tunneling, and the RFC says the table is input to a decision, not a verdict.

today: RFC 4097 is an Informational evaluation from 2005, and it is updated by RFC 8996. It is a record of how the MIDCOM protocol candidates compared, not a specification.

sections.title: What Was Evaluated and Why
sections.content:
MIDCOM stands for Middlebox Communications. A middlebox, such as a firewall or a NAT, enforces policy, and an application-aware MIDCOM agent asks it to open or change what is allowed. The framework is in RFC 3303 and the protocol requirements are in RFC 3304. This document checks whether an existing protocol could serve.

The process was simple: individuals volunteered to write an evaluation of one protocol each, and the list discussed them. The RFC admits that other protocols that might fit were left out because nobody volunteered to champion them. The five candidates were SNMP, RSIP, Megaco, Diameter and COPS.
sections.eli5: An app sometimes needs to politely ask a gatekeeper to open a gate. This memo asks which of five existing ways of talking to gatekeepers would work best.

sections.title: How Compliance Was Scored
sections.content:
Each protocol was checked against every MIDCOM requirement, grouped as protocol machinery, protocol semantics and general security requirements. Each result got one of four marks.

  • T: total compliance, the requirement is fully met.
  • P+: the requirement is fundamentally met through extensions such as packages or additional parameters.
  • P: some aspect is met, but the changes needed go beyond an extension or conflict with the design intent of the protocol.
  • F: the requirement is not met.

The RFC adds that the summary is not a conclusive statement of suitability. It is input to the overall decision process.
sections.eli5: It is a report card with four grades: yes, yes with a small add-on, partly, and no. Each protocol got a grade for each rule.

sections.title: SNMP and RSIP
sections.content:
SNMP was judged as SNMPv3 only, since SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c are Historic and have only trivial security. SNMP keeps intelligence in MIB modules rather than in the protocol, so a MIDCOM MIB module would be needed: requests are writes to managed objects and replies are changes the middlebox makes to them. A NAT MIB module (RFC 4008) already meets all NAT-control requirements except grouping of policy rules. For firewalls, existing SNMP work covered monitoring, not configuration.

RSIP (Realm Specific IP, RFC 3102 and RFC 3103) shares many framework elements with MIDCOM. But it always implicitly permits, makes no distinction between applications and agents, and has no policy decision points. Its tunnels between hosts and the middlebox mean the host sees public addresses and ports, but they need an RSIP server and a tunneling protocol in the middlebox and an RSIP client in each host.
sections.eli5: SNMP is a long-used way to read and set dials on devices, so it would need a new set of dials for firewalls. RSIP is a way of lending your computer an outside address, which turned out to need too many changes.

sections.title: Megaco, Diameter and COPS
sections.content:
Megaco (RFC 3015) is a master-slave protocol where Media Gateway Controllers control Media Gateways using terminations, contexts and packages. A Controller resembles the MIDCOM agent, but there is a catch: MIDCOM requires the agent to start the session, while Megaco has the gateway contact the controller.

Diameter (RFC 3588) is an AAA protocol with typed attribute-value pairs, and its IPFilterRule type may express MIDCOM policy rules. It was found to be a good fit, but possibly too heavy, and the evaluation notes that its RFCs had not yet been published at the time.

COPS (RFC 2748, and COPS-PR in RFC 3084) is a simple stateful query and response protocol over TCP between a policy server and its clients. The middlebox would act as the client and the agent as the server, so COPS has the same issue as Megaco with who starts the session.
sections.eli5: Megaco and COPS are used to a boss telling a worker what to do, but with the worker calling the boss first. MIDCOM wants the opposite. Diameter is a big toolbox where most tools would not be used.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.content:
Across all requirements, no protocol failed any. SNMP fully met 22 and partly met 5 through extensions. The RFC says SNMP meets all requirements with a suitable MIDCOM MIB module, is a full standard and has managed large networks. Its main restriction is the assumption that the policy decision point is part of the middlebox.

RSIP needs several additions, and its tunneling led the working group to find it unacceptable as the MIDCOM protocol. Megaco would need a new termination and package definition. Diameter shows a good overall fit but may be too heavy. COPS meets most requirements with its own extension methods, but would need local policy to let the PDP start the connection. On extension cost, SNMP and COPS-PR extend through MIBs and PIBs with no protocol impact, Diameter and Megaco need protocol changes, and RSIP has the largest impact.
sections.eli5: Nobody failed. SNMP came out on top for fitting the rules, but the memo says to treat the scores as advice, not as the final decision.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document adds no security analysis of its own. It says security considerations for the MIDCOM protocol are covered by the comparison against the security requirements of the MIDCOM requirements document, specifically in section 2.1.8 and section 2.3 of this evaluation. It also points out that SNMPv3 was chosen over earlier versions because it provides the security MIDCOM needs.
sections.eli5: The memo does not add new safety rules. It just checks each candidate against the safety rules that were already written down.
